reader_notes: Cold-solve reasoning: the chain is vacancy -> subdivision -> no vacancy. Six middle-aisle pews vacant in 1848 and four in 1849; by the 1851 plan the vacant marks are gone and the same boxes are ruled into single sittings at two shillings, with names crowding where one household stood. That the wardens split what would not let whole is the only conclusion the plans themselves carry, so B.
A is the trap for a reader who fixes on 'names crowd' and infers pressure on capacity; the recorded vacancies point the other way - demand for whole boxes was falling, not outstripping the building.
C is unsupported invention: the passage never says who took the single sittings, and the free benches are mentioned only as a price floor, not as a source of the new tenants.
D misreads the unit - two shillings is the price of one sitting, not of a whole box; a box cut into several sittings would fetch several times that.

The 1861 raise of the front boxes to a pound is a good discriminating detail rather than noise: the expensive boxes near the pulpit kept letting whole and even rose, which localises the failure to the middle aisle and keeps B from overreaching into 'the whole church was emptying'.

Friction point: 'falling row by row to three shillings at the west door, where the benches were free' made me re-read. On first pass the same location appears to carry both a three-shilling price and free seats; it resolves once you take the benches as a separate class of seat from the priced pews, but it costs a beat under exam time.

Smaller friction: 'and four the year after' leans on an 1849 plan that is never named. The opening ('each spring the churchwardens drew up a fresh plan') licenses it, but the sentence starts inside the 1848 plan and steps out of it without a seam.
The document-present / event-past tense scheme (the plan 'prices', pews 'are marked', the wardens 'raised') is handled consistently and reads as genuine antiquarian register, not as a slip.

'Tebbenholt' sits oddly among the surnames of an English parish - it reads Low-Countries or German rather than Victorian English. Harmless to the question, but it is the one word that felt manufactured.

No factual or internal-consistency problem found: the date sequence 1848 - 1849 - 1851 - 1856 - 1861 holds, and the pew economics (an eighteen-shilling box carrying three surnames by 1856, sittings at two shillings) are coherent with a box that could no longer be let entire.
